cim: Examining effectiveness of Ohio's AI training
cim_eredeti: Examining effectiveness of Ohio's AI training
szoveg_eredeti:
COLUMBUS, Ohio — Thousands of Ohioans are learning how to use artificial intelligence at work through a statewide training program. But whether those skills are leading to better jobs, higher pay or other measurable benefits remains an open question.

The AI Ready Ohio pilot program launched in Nov. 2025 through a partnership between JobsOhio and the Enterprise Technology Association. It aims to help Ohioans use AI to save time and money on the job.

For software developer Musa Hakim Jr., the training has helped him build on skills he was already using.

Hakim is developing an app designed to help teenagers set goals and track their progress. He uses AI to help improve the app and work through ideas.

He said the app had no one on its waitlist around this time last year. Now, he says, over 10,000 people are waiting to use it.

Hakim had already been using AI for approximately two years before taking AI Ready Ohio in August. He said the training helped him better understand how to use the technology responsibly, including setting rules for what AI can and cannot do within a company.

Summer Crenshaw, CEO and co-founder of the Enterprise Technology Association, said over 3,000 people have started the certification process, and over 2,000 have earned at least one certificate.

She said some participants are using what they learned to start businesses.

Crenshaw has also seen how AI can change the time and cost involved in developing software.

In 2015, she said, a team of 13 engineers spent six months and $1.5 million building a software platform for her business

Years later, she said she was able to recreate her business platform using generative AI in just one week for about $30.

But that example reflects Crenshaw’s own experience, not a measured outcome of the training program.

Bruce Weinberg, an economist at Ohio State University, said the number of certificates earned doesn’t necessarily show whether the training is improving people’s careers.

He said researchers could look at whether unemployed participants find jobs or whether those already working move into better-paying positions.

Some changes, such as finding employment, could be measured within months. Others, including wage growth, could take years to evaluate.

For now, Crenshaw says much of the evidence about how participants are using their training is anecdotal.

She hopes to survey participants at the end of 2027 to get a clearer picture of what has changed since they completed the program.

Hakim, meanwhile, hopes to expand his app to users in more states.

His experience offers one example of how AI training can be put to use. But whether the program is producing similar results for participants across Ohio remains to be seen.
